Then compare the best of each kind ## {.inverse .center} ::: {.notes} Compress: a penalty is a knob written into the objective. Two penalties, two bets. ::: ### Part 2: ridge and lasso ## Regularized (i.e. penalized) regression ::: {.notes} Legacy slide; its James--Stein opening is kept for later in the course, so the motivation here is week 4's early stopping. "Loss plus penalty" is the shape of most of today's methods. ::: Motivation: early stopping made the number of gradient-descent steps a knob that controlled how far the fit went. Can the knob be written into the objective instead? . . . For some penalty function $\mathcal P_\lambda$, which depends on a tuning parameter $\lambda$, the estimator $$\hat \beta_\lambda = \arg \min_\beta \| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|^2_2 + \mathcal P_\lambda(\beta)$$ is "regularized" or shrunk (shranken?) toward values that decrease the penalty. Often $\mathcal P_\lambda = \lambda \| \cdot \|$ for some norm . . . Many ML methods are optimizing "loss + penalty" ## Ridge (i.e. L2 penalized) regression ::: {.notes} Legacy slide, whole. This lambda is the course's lambda: the objective with the squared error not divided by n. glmnet divides the squared error by n and the ridge penalty by 2, so its lambda is this one over n up to that factor; the path figures' axes are glmnet's. Conventions, said once: the intercept is not penalized, and the columns are standardized before the penalty is applied (glmnet's default), since a penalty on beta_j depends on the units of x_j. ::: - Originally motivated by problems where $\mathbf X^T \mathbf X$ is uninvertible (or badly conditioned, i.e. almost uninvertible) - If $p > n$ then this always happens - Least squares estimator is undefined or numerically unstable For some constant $\lambda > 0$, $$\text{minimize } \| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|^2_2 + \lambda \| \beta \|^2$$ **Shrinks** coefficients $\hat \beta$ toward 0 Larger coefficients are penalized more (squared penalty) ## What $\lambda$ controls {minutes="3"} ::: {.notes} Exercise 2 derives the equations: the gradient of the penalized objective. Invertible for every positive lambda because X'X is positive semidefinite and lambda I adds lambda to every eigenvalue; that is "fitting when p > n". The figure: ridge on the Spotify training tracks, the eleven numeric inputs and five genre dummies, standardized; minus log lambda on glmnet's scale, so large lambda is on the left, every coefficient near zero; lambda to zero on the right, least squares (p = 16 < n here). Energy, duration and the pop and rap genres carry the largest coefficients. ::: ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="52%"} Set the gradient of $\| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|^2 + \lambda \| \beta \|^2$ to zero (exercise 2): $$ (\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda I)\,\hat\beta_\lambda = \mathbf X^T\mathbf y $$ $$ \hat\beta_\lambda = (\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda I)^{-1}\mathbf X^T\mathbf y $$ $\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda I$ is invertible for every $\lambda > 0$, whatever $n$ and $p$: one solution even when $p > n$ $\lambda \to 0$: least squares (when it exists). $\lambda \to \infty$: $\hat\beta_\lambda \to \mathbf 0$ ::: ::: {.column width="48%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/ridge-path-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: $\hat\beta_\lambda$ against $-\log\lambda$: the 16 standardized inputs (eleven numeric, five genre dummies), six named ::: ::: ## Lasso vs ridge: L1 vs L2 norm penalties ::: {.notes} Legacy slide, whole. Two forms; that they give the same family of solutions is a KKT fact and is not today's. The 1/2n is glmnet's scaling; the ridge slide did not divide by n. ::: A simple `diff` to remember lasso/ridge is via the penalty/constraint (1-norm instead of 2-norm). Lasso is $$\text{minimize } \frac{1}{2n}\| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|_2^2 \text{ s. t. } \| \beta \|_1 \leq t$$ where $\| \beta \|_1 = \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j|$. Lagrangian form $$\text{minimize } \frac{1}{2n} \| \mathbf y - \mathbf X \beta \|_2^2 + \lambda \| \beta \|_1$$ The lasso often gives estimates with many coefficients set to exactly zero ## Lasso vs ridge: solution paths of $\hat \beta$ ::: {.notes} The legacy figure's two panels, on the Spotify training tracks instead of the legacy simulation. Right panel, read left to right: at large lambda everything is zero, coefficients enter one at a time as lambda falls (energy and duration first, then instrumentalness and the pop genre), and several stay at exactly zero until far right. Left panel: every path shrinks toward zero and none sits at zero over an interval. Same inputs as the ridge slide. ::: ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/ridge-path-again-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/lasso-path-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: Spotify, the same 16 inputs, large $\lambda$ on the left. The lasso's coefficients are exactly zero over whole ranges of $\lambda$ and enter one at a time; ridge's are never zero ## {.inverse .center} ::: {.notes} Compress: one input, a curve instead of a line, two ways to get one; then one curve per input, added up. ::: ### Part 3: additive models ## Two ways to estimate a curve ::: {.notes} Week 1's data and week 1's k-NN, GDP per capita unlogged so that the relation is curved. Two ideas, named once: average nearby (k-NN; a kernel weights by distance instead of cutting at k), fit a basis (the next two slides; a penalty on it comes later in the course). We focus on the second; the first is a name. Both are curves, and both have a knob. Local regression (loess, ISLR 7.6) was a third panel here and is cut for time; it is skim reading only. ::: Life expectancy on GDP per capita, 142 countries in 2007 (no log this time). Two ways to turn a line into a curve ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/two-ways-1.png){width=1800} ::: ::: **Average nearby** ($k$-NN; a *kernel* weights by distance instead of cutting at $k$). **Fit a basis**: fixed curves, combined by least squares. We now focus on the second ## A spline is regression on basis functions ::: {.notes} ns() is in the splines package, which ships with R. Polynomials 1, x, x squared are a basis too, each global; a spline basis is built from pieces joined at knots. Natural cubic spline: cubic pieces between knots, two continuous derivatives at each knot, linear beyond the end knots; knots at quantiles of x. lm adds the intercept. ::: ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="48%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/spline-basis-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="52%"} A **basis**: fixed functions $b_1(x), \ldots, b_J(x)$ of one input, combined by least squares: $$ f(x) = \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^J \beta_j\, b_j(x) $$ linear in $\beta$: `ns(gdpPercap, df = J)` builds the $J$ columns for `lm()` A **natural cubic spline**: cubic pieces joined smoothly at knots, linear beyond the ends. The basis functions are the bends the knots allow; `lm` adds $\beta_0$ ::: ::: ## The basis size is the knob ::: {.notes} Same data, J = 2, 5, 15. J small, nearly a line; J large, wiggles, and at J = n the curve passes through every point with training error zero. Which J: the selection set, as for k and lambda. Later in the course a penalty on wiggliness replaces it, and J becomes a ceiling. ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/basis-size-1.png){width=1800} ::: ::: Small $J$: almost a line. Large $J$: the curve follows the points, and at $J = n$ it passes through every one (training error zero). Which $J$? The selection set, as for $k$ and $\lambda$. Later in the course: a penalty on wiggliness instead, with $J$ as a ceiling ## Additive modeling assumption ::: {.notes} Legacy slide. g is the link, identity today. One function per input, added up; a coefficient is the special case. Only the sum is determined, so each f_j is centered and the level sits in beta_0. ::: - **Linearity** assumption: each predictor has a *coefficient* $$g(\mathbb E[\mathbf y | \mathbf X]) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \mathbf x_1 + \beta_2 \mathbf x_2 + \cdots + \beta_p \mathbf x_p$$ - **Additivity** assumption: each predictor has a *function* $$g(\mathbb E[\mathbf y | \mathbf X]) = \beta_0 + f_1( \mathbf x_1) + f_2( \mathbf x_2) + \cdots + f_p(\mathbf x_p)$$ Includes linear models as special case if $f_j(\mathbf x_j) = \beta_j \mathbf x_j$ Today each $f_j$ is a spline with $J$ basis functions, so the whole model is one least-squares fit on $pJ$ columns: `lm(y ~ ns(x1, J) + ns(x2, J) + ...)`. The GAM in the reading is this model, with a link ## An additive model for popularity ::: {.notes} Spotify, the training tracks: six of the numeric inputs as splines with J = 4, genre as a factor, one least-squares fit on 30 columns. R squared about 0.17: most of popularity is not in these inputs, which is the honest state of affairs. Each panel is a fitted component, centered, over the middle 98 percent of its input. Read two: loudness (louder tracks score higher, 20 points across the range), release year (the oldest tracks score high, a low around 2012, then the steep rise into 2019 and 2020: recency, as the data note says). Energy falls once loudness is in the model: the two are correlated, and the component is what energy adds with loudness held fixed, week 2's reading. Backfitting, later in the course, is how these components are found when the one-input fits are not least squares. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_add <- lm(track_popularity ~ ns(loudness, 4) + ns(release_year, 4) + ns(danceability, 4) + ns(duration_min, 4) + ns(energy, 4) + ns(acousticness, 4) + genre, data = sp_train) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/spotify-components-1.png){width=1800} ::: ::: Each variable gets a curve instead of a coefficient (slope) ## {.inverse .center} ::: {.notes} Compress: a sequence of yes-or-no questions, each about one input, is a model too: a different shape altogether, rectangles with a constant in each; then why one tree is not enough and what averaging many does. ::: ### Part 4: trees and forests ## A regression tree for popularity ::: {.notes} The legacy penguin tree, on the Spotify training tracks: popularity on release year and energy (the year for its recency effect, energy as the strongest linear input on the lasso path), depth 3, at least 250 tracks in a leaf. Read it from the top: one question per node, the left branch is yes, a number in each leaf. The cutoff 2017.5 (2018 and later to the right) splits first; energy matters on both sides, with different cutoffs; the right side splits again at 2018.5. The leaf values are mean popularity in the leaf. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1-2"} fit_tree <- rpart(track_popularity ~ release_year + energy, sp_train, control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 3, cp = 0, minbucket = 250)) plot(fit_tree, uniform = TRUE, margin = 0.1) text(fit_tree, pretty = 0, cex = 1.9, digits = 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/spotify-tree-1.png){fig-align='center' width=92%} ::: ::: Left branch: yes. Leaves: mean popularity of the training tracks that reach them ## Regression tree predictions ::: {.notes} The same tree drawn in the input plane: each leaf is a rectangle, and the prediction is the mean popularity of the training tracks in it. A step function in two inputs, flat inside each rectangle: nothing smooth, nothing additive. The energy question is asked on both sides of 2018 with different cutoffs, which an additive model could not do. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/spotify-rectangles-1.png){fig-align='center' width=78%} ::: ::: Each leaf is a rectangle with one value; the training tracks in white. The three narrow strips on the right are the leaves for 2018 and for 2019 to 2020, split again by energy ## One predictor, every cutoff ::: {.notes} New slide, before the loop. One input, release year: for every cutoff, split the training tracks in two, predict each side's mean, and record the training MSE; the best cutoff is where the curve is lowest, 2018 here (the recency effect). The right panel is the two-leaf fit that cutoff gives: one question. Later in the course this is done by hand, scoring every cutoff in one pass. ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/best-cutoff-1.png){width=1800} ::: ::: For one input: try every cutoff, predict each side's mean, keep the cutoff with the smallest training MSE. One question, two leaves ## Recursive rectangular splitting on predictors ::: {.notes} Legacy slide, now the loop around the last slide: every input, its best cutoff, the best of those; then the same on each side. Greedy. How deep to grow and how to prune back come later in the course; today a depth is the tree's knob, chosen like the others. ::: "Stratification of the feature space" ``` Input: subset of data For each predictor variable x_j in subset Scan cutoff values to find the best split for x_j (last slide) Output: the predictor and cutoff with the best improvement ``` . . . Starting from the full dataset, compute the first split as above **Recurse**: take the two subsets of data from each side of the split and plug them both back into the same function Until some **stopping rule** prevents more splitting (today: a maximum depth, the tree's knob; growing deep and pruning back comes later in the course) ## A tree is unstable; a forest averages many ::: {.notes} New slide, before the fix. Gapminder, where 142 points make it visible: eight resamples of the countries (draws with replacement, the same size), a depth-3 tree and a J = 4 spline on each. The trees' cutoffs jump between resamples and their steps jump with them; the splines barely move. Across the grid the eight trees' predictions have an average standard deviation of about 1.6 years, the splines' about 0.9. A tree has high variance; the orange line, the average of the eight trees, is already smoother than any of them. Said, not derived: a random forest grows hundreds of trees, each on a resample of the training rows (these draws with replacement) with a random subset of the inputs offered at each split, and averages them: the orange line with hundreds of trees instead of eight. One model, more stable than any one tree, and no knob to tune today (the defaults). What the resampling and the random subsets do, how much averaging buys and what correlation costs: later in the course. ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/tree-variance-1.png){width=1800} ::: ::: The 142 countries resampled eight times, one fit per resample (blue). The trees' cutoffs jump with the sample; the splines barely move. Orange: the eight trees' average A **random forest** is a method that combines many trees into one model: hundreds of trees, each on a resample of the training rows, averaged (orange, with hundreds not eight). Today `randomForest()` with its defaults, no knob; details later in the course ## {.inverse .center} ::: {.notes} Compress: one more structure, built by composing what we have: a regression whose inputs are themselves regressions. ::: ### Part 5: neural networks ## A GLM of GLMs {minutes="3"} ::: {.notes} The whole idea on one slide, by analogy with what students know. A GLM (weeks 3 and 4): the inverse link applied to a linear predictor, g^{-1}(x^T beta). Iterate: feed the inputs into M logistic regressions, take their outputs as new inputs, and run a linear regression (or a logistic one, for a label) on those; all the weights are fitted together. The hidden units are a basis like part 3's, except that the basis is fitted to the data rather than fixed in advance, and each basis function uses all the inputs at once. Iterate again and the network is deep. Symbols: M hidden units, w_k the k-th unit's weights, g the logit link of week 4. Said, not on the slide: the hidden units are a basis like part 3's, fitted to the data along with the coefficients, each unit using every input at once. ::: A GLM: the inverse link applied to a linear predictor, $g^{-1}(\mathbf x^T\beta)$. Now iterate it ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="44%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/network-diagram-1.png){width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="56%"} **Hidden unit** $k$: a logistic regression of the inputs, with its own weights, $h_k(x) = g^{-1}(w_{k0} + w_k^T x)$, $g$ the logit link **Output**: a linear regression on the hidden units, $f(x) = \beta_0 + \sum_{k=1}^M \beta_k\, h_k(x)$ (logistic, for a label) A GLM whose inputs are $M$ GLMs. Iterate again: a *deep* network ::: ::: ## What to know about networks today ::: {.notes} Two things and no more. Fit: every weight at once, by gradient-based optimization on a loss with every feature of week 4's part 3 (not convex: the hilly road, the saddle); nnet() uses BFGS, a quasi-Newton method, rather than stochastic gradient descent, and linout = TRUE for a numeric outcome. The knob: M, chosen on the selection tracks; depth, and the penalty on the weights, are later knobs. nnet() ships with the base install; the rest of networks comes later in the course and in ST311. ::: **How it is fitted.** All $M(p + 1) + M + 1$ weights at once, by gradient-based optimization of a loss that is not convex: many valleys, with plateaus and saddles between them. Today's fits: `nnet()`, a quasi-Newton method **The knob.** $M$, the number of hidden units, chosen on the selection tracks. Depth, and a penalty on the weights: later knobs. In R, `nnet(size = M, linout = TRUE)` ## {.inverse .center} ::: {.notes} Compress: five families, five bets; three truths, one task, and the training error of every one of them. ::: ### Part 6: which structure? ## Comparison across three functional structures {minutes="3"} ::: {.notes} Ten inputs, uniform on minus one to one, noise sd 1, so the floor is an MSE of 1. The network: M chosen on the selection rows, a small fixed ridge penalty on its weights, fitted by nnet; with 300 rows it stays small. Truth A is a plane in three of the ten; B is three smooth one-input curves (f1 = -1 + 2x - x^2, f2 = sin(pi x), f3 = exp(-5(x - 1/2)^2)), scaled by 1.5, in three of the ten; C is one step that needs two inputs at once (signal variance 3, of which the best sum of one-input functions holds 2 and the product the last 1). Every knob chosen on the 100 selection rows, then the chosen fit refitted on the 400 training-plus-selection rows; the test set is 2,000 rows because the truth is simulated and we can afford it. Forest with its defaults, no knob. The ask: two minutes, a show of hands per truth; take the reasons, not only the names. ::: $p = 10$ inputs on $[-1, 1]$, $y = f^\star(x) + \varepsilon$, $\sigma^2 = 1$. Three truths: ::: {style="font-size: 0.92em"} - **A, sparse linear:** $f^\star(x) = 2x_1 - 1.5x_2 + x_3$ - **B, additive smooth:** $f^\star(x) = 1.5\,[f_1(x_1) + f_2(x_2) + f_3(x_3)]$: $f_1 = -1 + 2x - x^2$, $f_2 = \sin \pi x$, $f_3 = e^{-5(x - 1/2)^2}$ - **C, one step, two inputs at once:** $f^\star(x) = 4 \cdot \mathbf 1\{x_1 > 0,\ x_2 > 0\}$ ::: **One task.** 300 training, 100 selection, 2,000 test rows. Seven competitors: least squares; lasso ($\lambda$); $k$-NN ($k$); additive splines ($J$); a tree (depth); a forest; a network ($M$). Knobs chosen on the selection rows, refit on both, scored once ::: {.ask} For each truth: which family wins, which loses, and why? ::: ## Truth A: sparse linear, tall and then wide ::: {.notes} Left, tall: 300 training rows, 100 selection, refit on the 400. Least squares and the lasso sit on the floor (dotted line, the noise variance, the smallest population MSE; a realized test MSE on 2,000 rows can sit a little below it); the additive fit and the two-unit network are close, each with many more parameters to estimate; the forest and the tree pay for a shape they do not need; k-NN in ten dimensions is last. Right, wide: 100 training rows, 50 selection, refit on the 150, p = 200, the same truth. Least squares and the additive fit have no unique fit; the lasso alone stays near the floor; ridge, the forest and k-NN are near the mean's score; the two-unit network, with over 400 weights for 100 rows, fits the training rows exactly and is last. The hollow points: the forest's training error is a quarter of its test error; least squares' training error sits above its test error here (one realization; the theorem is about averages). ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/lb-A-1.png){width=1800} ::: ::: Dotted line: the noise variance, the smallest population MSE. For this sparse truth the lasso ties least squares when $n \gg p$, and alone stays near the floor when $p > n$ ## Truth B: additive smooth ::: {.notes} The additive fit near the floor, J = 3 chosen; the forest and the network behind it, then the tree, then the two planes, k-NN last. The forest can bend, but it bends with rectangles and needs many of them for a smooth curve; the plane cannot bend at all. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/lb-B-1.png){fig-align='center' width=75%} ::: ::: The additive fit was built for this truth. A forest can bend, with rectangles; a plane cannot bend at all ## Truth C: thresholds with an interaction ::: {.notes} The tree of depth 2 is the truth, so it sits on the floor; the forest close behind. A sum of one-input functions can hold at most two thirds of this signal (each input's share) and the smooth splines hold less than that, so the additive fit and least squares are far from the floor. The fitted network generalizes poorly here (one run; a network can approximate a step closely but this fit did not): the network and k-NN at the bottom. The tree's training error sits above its test error: another one-realization exception. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/lb-C-1.png){fig-align='center' width=75%} ::: ::: A sum of one-input functions can hold each input's share of this step, two thirds of the signal at best, and not the product. Two questions in a row hold all of it ## CTF competition: everyone on Spotify ::: {.notes} The baselines slide asked whether a shape could beat both; this is the answer on the selection tracks, the knobs chosen there. The two-unit network 486, additive splines 490 and the forest 493 lead; the tree 512; the lasso and least squares with genre 525; k-NN 528; least squares without genre 541; the mean 581. Least squares with genre is the fair comparison for the bending fits: same inputs, so the gap is the structure. The bars are each method's own standard error, not that of a difference, and the knobs were chosen on these same tracks, so the ranking is descriptive; the seminar's test set, with paired losses, is where differences get a standard error. The hollow points are the training scores: the forest's is 86, and that is right, not a bug: predict() on the training rows uses the trees that had each row in-bag, grown to leaves of five rows, so the forest nearly reproduces its training rows; its out-of-bag score, the honest in-sample number, is 475. The vault stays shut: the seminar refits on training plus selection and opens it once. What these data have: a nonlinear year effect and loudness, which the plane cannot bend to, and little else the inputs can see. ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05-1-structures_files/figure-revealjs/spotify-six-1.png){width=1650} ::: ::: Knobs chosen on the selection tracks, scored there. The three that can bend lead, close together and below the plane with the same inputs; the forest's training score is 86. The vault stays shut: the seminar refits and opens it once ## Four dimensions, not one {minutes="3"} ::: {.notes} Three minutes. Four questions about the world, not one scale from simple to complex: a truth can be tall and interactive, or wide and smooth. Each family is a bet on an answer; week 4's no free lunch says the bet is doing the work, and the selection set says which bet paid on these data (Spotify: smooth in year and loudness, roughly additive, so the splines, the forest and a two-unit network). k-NN near the bottom on every simulated truth: ten inputs of which seven are idle, 300 points, week 1's curse with a price on it; a rate on that price comes later in the course. ::: ::: {style="font-size: 0.94em"} | Axis | The question about $f^\star$ | Who bets which way | |---|---|---| | **wide or tall** | how $p$ compares with $n$ | least squares needs full column rank for one fit; the additive fit and a network overfit when $n$ is small; ridge and the lasso fit at any $p$ | | **sparse or dense** | how many inputs matter | the lasso bets few; least squares and ridge spread the fit over all; a forest tolerates idle inputs, $k$-NN pays for them | | **smooth or discontinuous** | how $f^\star$ moves with each input | splines, $k$-NN and networks bet smooth; trees bet on steps | | **additive or interactive** | whether inputs act separately | the additive fit bets separately; trees, forests, $k$-NN and networks allow interactions | : {tbl-colwidths="[22,30,48]"} ::: Four separate questions, not one scale from simple to complex. A family is a bet on the answers; a selection set says which bet paid ::: {.retrieval} Curse of dimensionality: $k$-NN near the bottom on every truth, seven idle inputs. No free lunch theorem: no family won every truth, and none can. ::: ## What the training error hides {minutes="3"} ::: {.notes} Two minutes for the ask; collect two orderings before the reveal. Why anyone cared: the training error is the only error you can compute without new data. The hollow points sat left of the filled ones on most rows, the forest's by a factor of four, and right of them on a few (least squares on truth A, the tree on truth C); the question is whether the usual direction is a law, and what the exceptions are. Expected answer after the theorem: it is a statement about averages over training sets, and one realization of 300 rows can go either way by a little; the test MSE is itself a noisy number. Week 4's symbols: a class, the best in it, what the data return. ::: On most rows of the leaderboards the training MSE sat below the test or selection MSE; on a few it sat above. Luck, or a law? Training data i.i.d. from the population; a class $\mathcal F$ fixed before the data; $f_{\mathcal F}$ the best in $\mathcal F$ (smallest $R$); $\hat f$ the empirical risk minimizer (smallest $\hat R_n$ over $\mathcal F$) ::: {.ask} Three numbers: $\mathbb E[\hat R_n(\hat f)]$, $R(f_{\mathcal F})$, $\mathbb E[R(\hat f)]$. Put them in order, and write down what you used. ::: ## Optimism theorem {minutes="3"} ::: {.notes} Stated; the three-line proof is exercise 1. The heuristic first: f-hat was chosen to make the training losses small, so it beats any fixed member of the class on the training data, and a fixed member's training error is unbiased for its risk (the one line that uses the sampling assumption); on the population f-hat cannot beat the best member. Chain the three. Covered: least squares, and a spline basis whose knots are fixed in advance (ns() places them at sample quantiles, so strictly the class depends on the data). Ridge and the lasso in their constrained form with a fixed radius t are minimizers over a fixed class; at a fixed lambda they are not (noiseless Y = X: ridge has positive training error while the best line has risk zero, so the left inequality fails). Not covered: a tree (greedy), a forest, k-NN, a network as fitted (the optimizer is not guaranteed to find the global empirical minimizer), and any knob chosen on the data. The direction was the usual one on the leaderboards, with exceptions, but the theorem is about the minimizer and about averages. ::: A function fixed before the data has an unbiased training error; $\hat f$ was chosen to make its own small, and cannot beat $f_{\mathcal F}$ on the population Training data i.i.d.; $\mathcal F$ fixed before the data; $\hat f$ the empirical risk minimizer over $\mathcal F$; $f_{\mathcal F}$ the best in $\mathcal F$ (risks finite, minimizers exist). Then $$ \mathbb E\big[\hat R_n(\hat f)\big] \;\le\; R(f_{\mathcal F}) \;\le\; \mathbb E\big[R(\hat f)\big] $$ ::: {.leave} Training error underestimates the risk: on average it sits below the best risk the class can reach, and the fitted model's risk above it. A test set estimates $R(\hat f)$; its average is the right end. ::: **Proof**: exercise 1 ## Before the seminar ::: {.notes} Say it once: the exercises are what the seminar's problems vary. The seminar's leaderboard is the Spotify task with every family; the test set is opened once, at the end. ::: - This week: exercises 1 and 2 at the top of the notebook. The optimism theorem's proof, three lines with numbered hints; and ridge's normal equations, with why $\mathbf X^T\mathbf X + \lambda I$ is invertible - In the seminar: the Spotify task with every family. Each knob chosen on the selection tracks, then the vault opened once for the leaderboard ## Conclusion: five bets, one task {.inverse} ::: {.notes} Compress: each family is a bet on the shape of f-star; the selection set says which bet paid; the training error says nothing you can trust, by a theorem. Next: how much flexibility, and how to choose it. ::: #### Each family is a bet on the shape of $f^\star$ A plane, a sparse plane, a sum of curves, a set of rectangles, an average of many, a composition. Four questions about the world decide which bet pays #### The data split decides what you may believe Fit on the training rows, tune on the selection rows, open the test set once #### Training error underestimates risk Optimistic on average for every minimizer over a fixed class

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
